'''Steven Peter Armes''' (born 1962)<ref name=companieshouse/> {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}}<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2014/steven-armes |title=Professor Steven Armes FRS |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |archive-date=2014-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502073329/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2014/steven-armes/ |author=Anon |year=2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  is a Professor of [[polymer chemistry]] and [[Colloid|colloid chemistry]] at the [[University of Sheffield]].<ref name="scopus">{{Scopus id}}</ref><ref name=people>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160127001017/http://armesresearch.group.shef.ac.uk/members.php|archive-date=2016-01-27|url=http://armesresearch.group.shef.ac.uk/members.php|title=Armes lab group members|first=Steven|last=Armes|year=2016|website=shef.ac.uk|location=Sheffield}}</ref>

==Education==
Armes was educated at [[Whitley Academy|Whitley Abbey Comprehensive School]]<ref name=whoswho/><ref name="whitley">{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2016|publisher=whitleyacademy.com|location=Coventry|url=http://www.whitleyacademy.com/school_information/alumni/Alumni_news/Professor_Steven_Armes.aspx|title=Whitley Academy Alumni: Professor Steven Armes|archive-date=2016-03-03|url-status=usurped|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303205304/http://www.whitleyacademy.com/school_information/alumni/Alumni_news/Professor_Steven_Armes.aspx}}</ref> in [[Coventry]] and the [[University of Bristol]] where he was awarded a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1983 followed by a [[PhD]] in 1987 for research supervised by Brian Vincent.<ref name=influences/><ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | title=Armes, Prof. Steven Peter | id = U281967 | year = 2017 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|author=Anon|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U281967|location=Oxford}}</ref><ref name=phd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=Steven Peter|last=Armes|title=Colloidal forms of conducting polymers|publisher=University of Bristol|year=1987|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/21850690?style=html|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.483279}}|authorlink=Steven Armes|oclc=499867741}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After a [[postdoctoral research]] at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]<ref name=orcid/> Armes became a lecturer at the [[University of Sussex]] in 1989<ref name=whoswho/> where he worked until 2004. He moved to Sheffield to become Professor of Polymer and Colloid Chemistry in 2004.<ref name=whoswho/> {{As of|2016}}, he is a director of Farapack Polymers Limited,<ref name=companieshouse/> a [[corporate spin-off]] from the University of Sheffield. Armes group does research on [[polymer chemistry]] and [[colloid chemistry]].<ref name=orcid>Steven Armes {{ORCID|0000-0002-8289-6351}}</ref> Using [[polymerization|polymerisation]] techniques such as [[reversible addition−fragmentation chain-transfer polymerization]] (RAFT) and [[atom-transfer radical-polymerization]] (ATRP) his laboratory synthesises a wide range of polymers.

His research focuses on the synthesis and application of polymers – long-chain molecules formed from many repeating units known as [[monomer]]s. In particular, Steven's research group has developed new ways to make water-soluble or water-dispersible polymers based on methacrylic monomers.<ref name=frs/>

A powerful approach is to use polymerization-induced [[self-assembly]] (PISA).<ref name="BlanazsArmes2009">{{cite journal|last1=Blanazs|first1=Adam|last2=Armes|first2=Steven P.|last3=Ryan|first3=Anthony J.|authorlink3=
Tony Ryan (scientist)|title=Self-Assembled Block Copolymer Aggregates: From Micelles to Vesicles and their Biological Applications|journal=Macromolecular Rapid Communications|volume=30|issue=4–5|year=2009|pages=267–277|pmid= 21706604 |issn=1022-1336|doi=10.1002/marc.200800713|doi-access=}}</ref> For example, a water-insoluble polymer can be grown from one end of a water-soluble polymer in aqueous solution. The growing [[hydrophobic]] chain leads to in situ self-assembly, forming [[copolymer]] nanoparticles of tuneable size and shape.<ref name="DuTang2005">{{cite journal|last1=Du|first1=Jianzhong|last2=Tang|first2=Yiqing|last3=Lewis|first3=Andrew L.|last4=Armes|first4=Steven P.|title=pH-Sensitive Vesicles Based on a Biocompatible Zwitterionic Diblock Copolymer|journal=[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]|volume=127|issue=51|year=2005|pages=17982–17983|issn=0002-7863|doi=10.1021/ja056514l|pmid= 16366531|bibcode=2005JAChS.12717982D }} {{closed access}}</ref> These nanoparticles have a wide range of potential applications, including as a long-term storage medium for stem cells, viscosity modifiers, novel microcapsules and nanoparticle lubricants.<ref name=frs/>

His other research interests include designing novel biocompatible copolymer gels and vesicles and developing microscopic nanocomposite particles, which have applications in paints and anti-reflective coatings. Steven also has a fruitful collaboration with [[space science|space scientists]] based in the United Kingdom, Germany, and the United States, for whom he designs synthetic mimics to aid our understanding the behaviour of [[micrometeorite]]s travelling at [[Hypervelocity|hypervelocities]] in outer space.<ref name=frs/> Armes has developed robust new synthetic routes to controlled-structure water-soluble polymers. He optimised the living radical polymerisation of [[hydrophilic]] [[methacrylate]]s, discovered a new class of 'schizophrenic' diblock [[copolymer]]s whose [[amphiphile|amphiphilicity]] can be switched on or off, and has designed a range of novel [[Biocompatible material|biocompatible]] block copolymer [[gel]]s and [[Vesicle (biology and chemistry)|vesicle]]s. His work on water-borne polymer colloids has led to novel shell cross-linked [[micelle]]s and [[nanocomposite]] particles, with applications in [[paint]]s, [[anti-reflective coating]]s and as [[emulsion|stimulus-responsive Pickering emulsifiers]].<ref name=royal/>

===Awards and honours===
Armes was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2014|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2014]].<ref name=frs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117101611/https://royalsociety.org/people/steven-armes-11000/ |archive-date=2015-11-17 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/steven-armes-11000/ |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |author=Anon |year=2014 |title=Professor Steven Armes FRS }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=2015-09-25 }}}}</ref> More recently, he has pioneered polymerisation-induced [[self-assembly]] to produce a range of bespoke spherical, worm-like and vesicular [[nanotechnology|nano-objects]] via RAFT dispersion polymerisation.<ref name="royal"/> In 2013, Armes was awarded the [[Tilden Prize]] by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="The University of Sheffield 2021">{{cite web | title=Armes, FRS, Steven P., Professor | website=The University of Sheffield | date=14 December 2021 | url=https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/chemistry/people/academic/steven-p-armes-frs | access-date=27 August 2022}}</ref>
